messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 30
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Software Engineer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 46

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event, Olfactory (Sweat/Body): Sweat or body odour, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Threat: Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Memory: Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Priya Shah is a 30-year-old software engineer who came to treatment after months of worsening sleep and a growing sense that her apartment never felt fully secure, no matter how many times she checked it. She is married and lives with her husband in a city high-rise, working mostly in person now after several years of remote work. In the first sessions, she spoke haltingly about childhood physical abuse by a caregiver, describing not a single discrete incident but a cluster of scenes from home that still felt dangerous in her body even when she could not lay them out in order. What stayed with her most sharply were sensory fragments: the sour-salty taste that would fill her mouth when she was crying, the smell of sweat from being held too close, and the smell of alcohol on the caregiver’s breath as she tried to guess from one moment to the next whether she was about to be hit.

She did not remember these experiences as a coherent story. When she tried to explain what happened, she would start with one image, jump abruptly to another, and then lose track of what came first. She would say she knew there had been shouting, being grabbed, the alcohol smell leaning over her, but once the memory began to come back she became so flooded that she had to stop speaking and look away. Often she pushed the memory away before it got to the worst part, as if finishing it would be intolerable. Even in session, she seemed to brace against something just beyond reach.

Those fragments are easily stirred in her current life. At work, when she squeezes past colleagues after a long day and catches body odor in a crowded elevator, her chest tightens before she can think. If a coworker returns from a happy hour and the smell of beer lingers in a conference room, she becomes instantly alert, scanning the room and feeling unable to settle back into her code. Sometimes an ordinary taste will do it—something metallic or sour in the back of her mouth when she has skipped lunch and had too much coffee—and suddenly she is no longer just in the office. In those moments the sensory cue pulls up pieces of the old scenes, and with them comes the same conviction that she is not safe. She comes home keyed up, checks the deadbolt repeatedly, tests the windows, and still cannot relax on the couch beside her husband.

The memories themselves deepen that sense of danger. When they break through, they do not arrive as finished recollections but as disordered, unbearable shards, and Priya is left with the feeling that something threatening is present without being fully known. At night this is worst. She lies in bed trying not to think, but the partial images press in anyway—the smell, the crying, a hand gripping her arm—and because she cannot bring the memory to a clear end, her body acts as if the threat is ongoing. She gets up to check the front door again, then the balcony lock, then returns to bed only to listen for sounds in the hallway. She tells herself she knows she is a married adult in a secure apartment, yet she cannot make herself believe it enough to rest.

Over time, her efforts to stay on guard have also shaped how the memories return. She has become so practiced at monitoring for danger—listening for movement outside the door, noticing smells immediately, staying tense in her own home—that small sensory details now stand out to her with unusual force. A trace of sweat on the subway or alcohol on someone passing her on the sidewalk can set off a rush of half-memory. Because she meets these moments already braced, the recollections feel even more overwhelming, and she cuts them off before they can unfold. The more she tries to keep herself safe by staying vigilant and never letting down her guard, the more fragmented and intrusive the memories seem to become.

There is also a way the memories have made the triggers stronger. Priya has come to associate those smells and tastes so closely with being trapped and powerless that they now feel contaminated in themselves. She avoids team outings at bars and leaves shared rides if another passenger smells of alcohol. In crowded office spaces she keeps her distance, not wanting to risk catching someone’s body odor and feeling that sudden internal drop. Her husband has noticed that she insists on controlling the home environment at night—checking locks, rechecking them, pausing in the doorway as if listening for something—and that she seems exhausted but unable to settle. Their evenings have narrowed around her rituals and her sleeplessness.

What finally brought her in was a recent week in which she barely slept, started making mistakes at work, and found herself crying in the restroom after catching the smell of beer on a client visiting the office. She was frightened by how quickly she could feel like a terrified child while knowing, intellectually, that nothing was happening. More than anything, she fears that she will never be able to let her guard down, never be able to remember what happened without being overwhelmed, and never again experience her own home or her own body as fully safe. She says, quietly, that she hopes therapy might help her “put it in order” enough to sleep.
